nodes.label: Funder landscape
nodes.one_line: Sort any potential funder into the federal, foundation, corporate, or regranting pipeline and know which documents, timelines, and constraints each one implies.
know_what: Federal grants — discretionary awards through Grants.gov and SAM.gov, governed by 2 CFR 200, with page limits, scored review, and fixed submission windows
Foundations — private, family, community, and corporate foundations tracked in Candid's Foundation Directory, applying via LOI and full proposal on their own cycle
Regranting intermediaries — organizations that pass larger awards down (e.g., state arts agencies, United Ways), often with simpler applications but narrower scope
Corporate giving programs — company-run grants and sponsorships tied to brand, employee engagement, and geographic footprint
Formula vs discretionary funding — formula funds arrive by statute and eligibility; discretionary funds are competed and won
General operating vs project support — unrestricted operating money vs restricted project money, and which funder types typically offer which
Cycle length — federal cycles of 6-18 months from NOFO to award vs foundation cycles that can turn in 2-4 months
Review burden — federal reviewers score against published criteria; foundation staff and boards decide on mission fit
know_how: Classify any funder by pipeline (federal / foundation / corporate / regranting) in one sentence, naming the documents it expects
Check a federal opportunity's Assistance Listing number and agency to confirm who is really the funder
Read a foundation's 990-PF or 990 to classify it as private, family, or community and note its giving pattern
Determine the entry point — LOI, full proposal, or simple form — from the funder type before drafting anything
Estimate the timeline implied by the funder type and put it on the calendar before drafting
Match funder type to need: general operating support usually comes from foundations, big project dollars from federal agencies
habits: Before any outreach, name the funder type out loud and state the entry document it expects
Keep a one-line taxonomy note on every funder record in your pipeline tracker
When a new funder appears, classify it before evaluating fit
Recheck classifications annually — foundations change focus, corporate programs pivot
When a funder's behavior contradicts your classification, note it and adjust rather than forcing the fit
File every funding notification under its pipeline so past research is reusable
nodes.checkpoint: Given descriptions of five real funders (a federal agency, a private foundation, a community foundation, a corporate giving program, a regranting intermediary), classify each and name its entry document and typical timeline with no errors.
nodes.common_failure: Treating all funders as one pipeline: drafting a federal-style narrative for a foundation that wanted a one-page LOI, or vice versa. The taxonomy collapses and the wrong document gets written.
sources: Candid Foundation Directory
Grants.gov
Karsh & Fox, The Only Grant-Writing Book You'll Ever Need

nodes.label: Candid foundation search
nodes.one_line: Search the Candid Foundation Directory by geography, focus area, and giving history to build a real list of foundations that could fund your work.
know_what: Candid Foundation Directory (formerly Foundation Directory Online) — the searchable database of U.S. foundations with grants, 990s, and contact data
990-PF and 990 — the IRS filings that reveal a foundation's actual grantmaking: recipients, amounts, trustees
ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer — free digitized 990s when you don't have a Candid subscription
Grants to organizations vs individuals — most directories distinguish them; you usually want organizational grantmakers
Giving interests — the coded subjects, geographies, and populations a foundation funds
Typical grant size — the low/high/average award that tells you whether an ask is realistic
Submission type — the foundation's stated entry point: LOI, full proposal, or no unsolicited requests
Deadlines and cycles — board meeting dates and whether the foundation accepts rolling applications
know_how: Build a search from your program's subject, geography, and population filters in the Foundation Directory
Verify each shortlist foundation's recent giving in 990s before spending time on fit
Export a shortlist with contact info, focus areas, and giving range into your pipeline tracker
Check the recent-grants view (or 990 Schedule I) to see if the foundation already funds your type of organization
Note the submission type and cycle on each record so you never cold-submit where LOIs are required
Cross-check Candid data against the foundation's own website for the current year's priorities
habits: Search in batches, then verify with 990s, rather than trusting the marketing description
Log every foundation you research into the tracker in the same session you research it
Refresh your search quarterly — new foundations appear and giving interests shift
Save every successful search as a template so re-running it takes minutes, not hours
Verify a foundation's current priorities against its website before the first contact
nodes.checkpoint: Produce a verified shortlist of 10 foundations likely to fund your program, each with giving range, submission type, and evidence from a 990 or the foundation's own materials.
nodes.common_failure: Building a list from a foundation's aspirational website copy instead of its actual 990s — the list looks plausible and funds nothing.
sources: Candid Foundation Directory
ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer
Foundation Center (now Candid) training materials

nodes.label: Funder-fit triage
nodes.one_line: Read a funder's stated priorities, past awards, and restrictions to judge whether a project is a genuine fit before spending hours writing.
know_what: Fit vs wish — the difference between a funder whose priorities genuinely match and one you merely want money from
Priorities and focus areas — the foundation's stated current interests, usually on its website and annual report
Giving history — what the foundation actually funded last year, visible in 990s and Candid grant records
Restrictions — geographic limits, entity-type limits, no-unsolicited policies, no capital campaigns, no regranting
Funding strategy — many small grants, few large ones, or running its own initiatives
Relationship stage — whether the foundation requires an introduction, an LOI, or accepts direct proposals
Alignment evidence — the concrete overlaps (populations, geography, methods) you can cite in an approach
know_how: Score fit on three axes — mission, geography, and ask size — before writing anything
Check the foundation's own list of things it does not fund against your project line by line
Read the last two years of grants (990 schedules or Candid) and look for your field, geography, or org type
Look for a pattern of repeat grantees — some foundations effectively fund a closed circle, which changes your odds
Identify the decision maker — staff program officer, board committee, or giving committee — and how they take input
Write a one-paragraph fit statement for a go candidate, or a one-line no-go reason and move on
habits: Never draft before fit: the fit check comes first, always
Keep the no-go list as deliberate as the go list — it protects your hours
Recheck fit when a new RFP or LOI window opens; priorities change quarterly
Write the no-go reason on the funder record so you never re-litigate it
When a maybe goes to go, capture what changed so the pattern is visible
nodes.checkpoint: Given five foundation profiles, classify each as go / maybe / no-go with a written reason, and the go list survives a program officer's 'why us' interrogation.
nodes.common_failure: Convincing yourself a funder fits because the money is attractive — the hours go into a proposal that a program officer rejects as off-mission in one read.
sources: Candid Foundation Directory
Jane Geever, The Foundation Center's Guide to Proposal Writing
Karsh & Fox, The Only Grant-Writing Book You'll Ever Need

nodes.label: Problem statement
nodes.one_line: State the problem your project exists to solve in one paragraph with named evidence, so a stranger reviewer understands why the work matters.
know_what: Problem statement — the opening paragraph(s) that establish the need your project addresses, with evidence
Population of focus — who exactly is harmed or underserved, named specifically rather than 'the community'
Magnitude — the scale of the problem in numbers: counts, rates, percentages, with citations
Consequence — what happens if the problem persists, in terms a reviewer can picture
Root cause vs symptom — the underlying driver vs its surface effects
Local evidence — data specific to your geography or population that national statistics miss
Gap in services — the specific absence your project fills, which is what justifies funding you rather than someone else
know_how: Open with the population and the scale of the problem in the first sentence, not with your organization's history
Cite at least one authoritative statistic per claim, with source and year
Narrow from national to local: the national trend, then your city or county's numbers
State the consequence of inaction so the reviewer feels the cost of not funding
Close the paragraph by pointing at the gap your project fills
Cut adjectives and let the numbers and the named population carry the weight
habits: Draft the problem statement before the project description, and revise it last
Every statistic in the statement must have a source you could produce on request
Re-read the statement asking whether a stranger in another field would find it urgent
Keep a running file of strong need statistics so drafting starts from evidence, not memory
When the program changes, re-check that the statement still describes the real problem
nodes.checkpoint: Write a problem statement that a reviewer outside your field can summarize back to you accurately after one read, with every statistic cited.
nodes.common_failure: Starting with your organization's history or the project's features instead of the problem, so the need — the thing being funded — never gets established.
sources: Community Tool Box — Defining the Problem
Karsh & Fox, The Only Grant-Writing Book You'll Ever Need
Beverly Browning, Grant Writing For Dummies

nodes.label: Theory of change
nodes.one_line: Write the if-then chain from your activities to the long-term change you claim, exposing the assumptions a reviewer will test.
know_what: Theory of change — the explicit if-then chain from your activities to the long-term change you claim
Outcomes pathway — the sequence: activities → immediate outcomes → intermediate outcomes → long-term change
Assumptions — the beliefs about how change happens that your chain depends on
Preconditions — the conditions that must already hold for your intervention to work
Backwards mapping — starting from the long-term goal and working backwards to what must be true before it
Indicators at each step — the observable evidence that a link in the chain actually fired
Causal vs correlational claims — 'this produced that' vs 'these happened together'
know_how: Start from the long-term change and ask 'what must be true before this?' repeatedly until you reach your activities
Write each link as an if-then sentence and mark the assumption each one rests on
Test the chain for jumps — a link that skips from 'training' to 'higher employment' without intermediate outcomes
List the preconditions your project assumes: staffing, partner cooperation, participant attendance
Keep the theory to one page; the full narrative detail belongs in the logic model
Ask a skeptical reader to attack the weakest link and revise it
habits: Ask 'why will this work?' before 'how will we do it?' on every new project
Write assumptions down — unwritten assumptions get discovered by reviewers, painfully
Re-examine the theory when results don't match it, instead of moving the goalposts
Show the one-page theory to a practitioner who does the work and ask what link is weakest
Keep a library of theories of change from strong proposals in your field

know_why.claim: Every serious proposal needs an explicit theory of change, even for small grants.
know_why.because: it exposes the assumptions and the activity-outcome chain that reviewers actually score, and it keeps the proposal internally consistent.
know_why.disputed_by: pragmatic grant writers who argue that for small foundation grants a one-page logic model or a well-evidenced problem statement is enough, and that formal theory-of-change work consumes hours with little review payoff.
know_why.source: Aspen Institute Roundtable on Community Change & ActKnowledge, Theory of Change resources

nodes.checkpoint: Produce a one-page theory of change for your project with a complete if-then chain, every assumption named, and no jump from activity to long-term outcome.
nodes.common_failure: Writing a chain that's really a list of activities ending in a wish — no intermediate outcomes, no assumptions — so the theory can't be tested or scored.
sources: ActKnowledge / Aspen Institute Roundtable on Community Change — Theory of Change materials
Ann Emery — theory of change and evaluation writing
W.K. Kellogg Foundation Logic Model Development Guide

nodes.label: Logic model
nodes.one_line: Turn your theory into the inputs-activities-outputs-outcomes table funders expect, with every column traceable to the next.
know_what: Logic model — the inputs → activities → outputs → outcomes → impact table derived from the theory of change
Inputs — the resources you commit: staff, funding, facilities, partners
Activities — what the project does: workshops, services, campaigns, coaching
Outputs — the countable units produced: sessions held, people served, materials distributed
Outcomes — the changes in participants that result, short- and long-term
Impact — the longer-term population-level change the project contributes to
Column traceability — the discipline that every output connects to an activity and every outcome to an output
know_how: Derive the model from the theory of change rather than filling a template with whatever fits
Write one row per activity cluster: activity → its outputs → its outcomes, keeping columns aligned
Distinguish outputs (we served 120 people) from outcomes (attendance improved by X)
Put measurable language in the outcome column so indicators can hang off it later
Keep the model to one page; reviewers read it as a map, not an essay
Cross-check that every outcome in the model appears in the proposal's objectives and evaluation plan
habits: Build the logic model before the budget, so the budget funds the activities in the model
Update the model when the program changes, not at report time
Use the model as the table of contents for the evaluation section
Run a monthly trace: pick any outcome column and confirm the activities feeding it still exist
When a funder supplies its own model format, translate yours into it rather than inventing a parallel one

know_why.claim: A logic model must be built from the theory of change, not from a template.
know_why.because: template-first models produce columns of plausible-looking outputs with no outcome chain behind them, and reviewers cut them as boilerplate.
know_why.disputed_by: funder scorecards that request 'a logic model' as a compliance artifact and accept any reasonable table, which trains applicants to fill templates.
know_why.source: W.K. Kellogg Foundation Logic Model Development Guide

nodes.checkpoint: Build a one-page logic model where a stranger can trace any output back to an activity and any outcome forward to impact, with no dead-end columns.
nodes.common_failure: Filling in a template so the model is complete but disconnected — outputs that match no activity, outcomes that match no output — which reviewers read as a sign of sloppy program design.
sources: W.K. Kellogg Foundation Logic Model Development Guide
University of Wisconsin–Extension Logic Model resources (Ellen Taylor-Powell)
Innovation Network, Logic Model Workbook

nodes.label: SMART objectives
nodes.one_line: Write objectives that are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound so your outcomes can be evaluated at closeout.
know_what: SMART — specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound; the standard shape for a grant objective
Objective vs activity — an objective states the change to be achieved; an activity states what you will do
Baseline — the starting value you measure against, without which 'increase' is meaningless
Target — the numeric destination: 'from 40% to 60%' rather than 'improve attendance'
Time-bound — the date or period by which the objective is met, usually the grant period
Outcome-level objectives — objectives that describe participant change, not staff activity
know_how: Write each objective as one sentence: by [date], [population] will [measurable change] from [baseline] to [target]
Run each objective through the five SMART letters and rewrite anything that fails one
Check achievability against your staffing and timeline before committing to a number
Make objectives outcome-level: 'participants will complete the course' is an output, not an objective
Align every objective to a row in the logic model so the proposal hangs together
Limit to 3-5 objectives; more than that reads as overreach and becomes unverifiable
habits: Before drafting, list the baseline numbers you already have — or plan to collect them
Every objective gets a 'who measures it and when' note before it goes in the proposal
Review objectives against results at midpoint, not just at closeout
Keep the baseline numbers attached to each objective so the target is never orphaned
When asked to cut objectives to fit a page, cut the least measurable one first

know_why.claim: SMART phrasing is the unit reviewers actually score, so objectives must be written that way even when the work is qualitative.
know_why.because: a measurable, time-bound objective is the only part of a narrative that can be checked at closeout, and reviewers reward claims they can verify.
know_why.disputed_by: evaluators who argue objectives-first planning locks in the wrong outcomes, and that programs should start from the change sought and choose metrics to fit rather than force the change into a SMART template.
know_why.source: George T. Doran, 'There's a S.M.A.R.T. Way to Write Management's Goals and Objectives' (1981)

nodes.checkpoint: Rewrite a vague project description into 3-5 SMART objectives, each with baseline, target, date, and a named measure, that survive a reviewer's 'how will you know?' challenge.
nodes.common_failure: Objectives that restate activities ('we will run 12 workshops') as if that were a result — nothing is measurable, so the evaluation section has nothing to hang on.
sources: George T. Doran (1981), 'There's a S.M.A.R.T. Way to Write Management's Goals and Objectives'
Community Tool Box — Writing SMART objectives
Beverly Browning, Grant Writing For Dummies

nodes.label: Proposal outline
nodes.one_line: Map your full proposal against the funder's stated sections and page limits before writing a word, so nothing gets written that can't be used.
know_what: Funder outline — the section-by-section structure the funder specifies: narrative, budget, attachments
Page limits — hard caps per section (e.g., NIH's 12-page research strategy, many foundations' 10-page total) that the outline must respect
Review criteria order — the scoring criteria (significance, approach, personnel, evaluation) that should drive section order
Content budget — the allocation of pages to sections by the weight of the criteria
Boilerplate inventory — reusable sections (org overview, personnel, prior success) you can drop in
Gap list — the sections that need new writing vs ones that can be assembled from existing material
know_how: Copy the funder's required sections verbatim into an outline document before writing anything
Assign each criterion to the section that will answer it, and note where in the section
Allocate pages proportionally to criteria weight, not to your interest
Mark each section as draft-ready, needs-writing, or needs-data so you know the real work
List the required attachments and who owns each one
Set the outline as the roadmap: no prose until every section has a bullet list of what it must contain
habits: Outline first, always — a proposal written without an outline gets rewritten
Keep a boilerplate folder current so the outline can pull from it
Re-outline when a funder changes its requirements mid-cycle
Keep a reusable master outline per funder so the next proposal starts from a known shape
Time-box the outline: if it takes more than a couple of hours, the funder's requirements are still unclear
nodes.checkpoint: Given a real NOFO or foundation guidelines, produce a section-by-section outline with a page allocation per section that sums to the page limit, and a named owner for each attachment.
nodes.common_failure: Writing the narrative first and fitting it to the outline afterwards — page limits get blown and criteria get answered implicitly instead of in their own sections.
sources: NIH — Write Your Application guidance
Karsh & Fox, The Only Grant-Writing Book You'll Ever Need
Grants.gov application guides

nodes.label: Project narrative
nodes.one_line: Write the narrative body — need, approach, personnel, evaluation — that answers the funder's review criteria in order.
know_what: Project narrative — the main body: need, approach, personnel, evaluation, sustainability, written to the funder's criteria
Approach — the methods and activities, sequenced, with who does what
Need section — the problem statement plus local evidence, tailored to this funder
Personnel — who will do the work and why they are qualified, often with brief bios
Evaluation section — how success will be measured, tied to the objectives
Sustainability — how the work continues after the grant, increasingly required
Voice — the funder's reading level and culture: federal reviewers want precision, foundation staff want the mission
know_how: Answer the review criteria in order, using the criteria's own headings as section headers
Open each section with the claim, then the evidence, then the connection to the project
Quote the funder's language back where appropriate — mirror their terms for the work
Show, don't tell: name the population, the numbers, the method, the timeline
Weave the logic model's outcomes into the narrative so the document and the table agree
Write to the page limit: if the cap is 10 pages, deliver 9.5, not 10 pages of padding
habits: Draft section by section against the outline, then read the whole as one document
Check every claim in the narrative against the budget — the numbers must match
Read the narrative aloud; if a sentence survives only because you wrote it, cut it
Track which sections you cut under pressure so the next outline weights them correctly
Keep one example of a past winning narrative in your field as a yardstick for density
nodes.checkpoint: Produce a complete project narrative under the funder's page limit where a reviewer can find each published criterion answered in its own section with evidence.
nodes.common_failure: Writing the narrative as an essay about the organization instead of an argument to the criteria — reviewers can't find the answers they're paid to score.
sources: NIH — Write Your Application
Carlson & O'Neal-McElrath, Winning Grants Step by Step
Karsh & Fox, The Only Grant-Writing Book You'll Ever Need

nodes.label: Budget construction
nodes.one_line: Build a line-item project budget with personnel, fringe, travel, equipment, and other categories that sums correctly and tells the project's story.
know_what: Line-item budget — the standard format: personnel, fringe, travel, equipment, supplies, contractual, other, indirect
Cost categories — the 2 CFR 200 categories federal reviewers expect to see
Direct vs indirect costs — costs attributable to the project vs the organization's shared overhead
Personnel — salaries and wages, priced as percent effort or hours times rate
Fringe — the employer-side costs (payroll taxes, benefits) added to salary
Matching funds — required or pledged contributions, cash or in-kind, shown in the budget
Reconciling totals — column sums and grand total that are exact and cross-checkable
know_how: Build the budget in a spreadsheet with a formula for every total, never a hand-typed number
Start from the logic model's activities so every line funds something in the model
Use realistic rates: actual salaries, actual vendor quotes, not round numbers
Show percent effort for each person so reviewers see the staffing story
Add a notes column explaining each line as you build it — that becomes the budget narrative
Reconcile the budget to the narrative numbers before submission
habits: Budget from quotes and payroll, not from 'we probably need' guesses
Update the budget whenever the program design changes
Keep last year's budget as a template with formulas intact
When a line exceeds your mental benchmark, question the program design before inflating the number
Run the budget past the person who will actually spend it before it ships
nodes.checkpoint: Build a line-item project budget with all standard categories, exact totals, percent effort per person, and no line that a reviewer can't trace to the program.
nodes.common_failure: A budget that doesn't sum, or sums only because numbers were fudged — reviewers check the math, and round-number guesses signal an unserious budget.
sources: 2 CFR 200 (Uniform Guidance) cost principles
Grants.gov budget guidance
Foundation Center — Budgeting for Grants materials

nodes.label: Budget narrative
nodes.one_line: Write the justification that explains each line item to a reviewer who wasn't in the room when you planned it.
know_what: Budget narrative — the written justification that explains each line item to a reviewer
Justification — for each line: what it is, why it's needed, how the amount was derived
Personnel justification — role, effort percentage, and the calculation behind the salary
Travel — destination, number of trips, cost basis (per-diem rates, airfare quotes)
Equipment vs supplies — the threshold and the distinction reviewers enforce
Indirect cost explanation — the rate used and its basis: negotiated agreement, funder cap, or 10% de minimis
Match documentation — how the match will be met and evidenced
know_how: Write one paragraph per line item in the same order as the budget
Show the math: '2 trips x $800 airfare + $160 per-diem x 3 days'
Justify need, not just amount: a line is defensible when the reviewer sees why the project can't run without it
State the indirect basis explicitly — negotiated rate agreement, 10% de minimis, or funder cap
Cross-reference the narrative: 'as described in the project narrative, page 4'
Keep to the funder's length expectation — usually 1-2 pages; some federal programs want more
habits: Write the narrative from the budget notes column you kept while building the budget
Every number in the narrative must match the budget exactly
Re-read the narrative pretending you're a skeptical grants officer
Update the narrative the moment a budget line changes, so the two never drift apart
Keep a copy of the funder's cost principles open while writing the justification
nodes.checkpoint: Produce a budget narrative where every line item has a calculation and a need-based justification, and an auditor can recompute every total from the text.
nodes.common_failure: Repeating the budget as prose ('we request $5,000 for supplies') without the calculation or the why — the justification that makes the line credible is missing.
sources: 2 CFR 200 cost principles
NIH SF424 budget instructions
Carlson & O'Neal-McElrath, Winning Grants Step by Step
